title: Unscented Kalman Filtering for 3D Orientation Estimation
subtitle: Quaternion UKF with IMU calibration and motion-capture validation
summary: Quaternion UKF for 3D attitude tracking from IMU data, with gravity-consistent accelerometer calibration, gyro scale/bias alignment to motion-capture ground truth, and manifold-aware estimation.

glance.oneLiner: Quaternion UKF for IMU-only 3D orientation tracking with motion-capture calibration and validation.
glance.problem: Estimate 3D orientation from noisy, biased IMU measurements on a nonlinear rotation manifold, while using motion-capture ground truth to calibrate sensors and validate the filter.
glance.approach: I calibrated accelerometer and gyroscope axes with affine models, then ran a quaternion UKF that represents orientation uncertainty in a 3D tangent space and propagates sigma points through nonlinear dynamics and measurement models.
glance.results: The filter tracks motion-capture orientation closely when bias/scale are calibrated, and reveals drift or sign errors quickly through roll/pitch/yaw comparisons.
takeaways: Sensor calibration dominates orientation accuracy and drift behavior.
Quaternion-aware averaging is essential for valid UKF updates.
Axis conventions and sign flips are easy to miss without ground truth.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: This work implements a quaternion-based Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for 3D attitude tracking using IMU measurements (accelerometer + gyroscope), with motion-capture orientations used offline as ground truth for calibration and validation.

The pipeline has two core components: sensor calibration from raw ADC units to physical units, and nonlinear state estimation on the quaternion manifold using an unscented transform with quaternion-consistent averaging.

sections.title: Theoretical Breakdown
paragraphs: Sensor calibration starts from the affine conversion used for both accelerometer and gyroscope, $$\text{value} = (\text{raw} - \text{bias})\,\frac{3300\,\text{mV}}{1023\cdot \text{sensitivity}}.$$ For the accelerometer, I treat the expected specific force as gravity in the body frame and compute $$\mathbf{a}^{\text{true}}_t = R_t\,\mathbf{g}, \quad \mathbf{g} = [0, 0, 9.81]^{\top}\,\text{m/s}^2.$$ I then fit a per-axis linear model $a^{\text{true}} \approx x_0\,a^{\text{raw}} + x_1$ via least squares and recover $$\text{sensitivity} = \frac{3300\,\text{mV}}{1023\,x_0}, \quad \text{bias} = -\frac{x_1}{x_0}.$$ To reduce noise, I keep only samples with sufficient gravity projection per axis and validate calibration with roll/pitch estimates, $$\hat{\phi} = \mathrm{atan2}(a_y, a_z), \quad \hat{\theta} = \mathrm{atan2}(-a_x, \sqrt{a_y^2 + a_z^2}).$$
Table 1 summarizes the calibrated bias and sensitivity values used for both sensors. Keeping them explicit makes it clear how the affine conversion maps raw ADC counts into physical units.

Gyroscope calibration uses motion-capture rotations to derive angular velocity. Given successive rotations, $$\Delta R_t = R_{t+\Delta} R_t^\top,$$ I map $\Delta R_t$ to a quaternion $q = (q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3)$, compute $$\theta = 2\,\arccos(q_0), \quad \hat{\mathbf{x}} = (q_1, q_2, q_3),$$ and approximate $$\boldsymbol{\omega}^{\text{true}}_t \approx \frac{\hat{\mathbf{x}}\,\theta}{\Delta t}.$$ I select $\Delta t \approx 0.15$ s to avoid noisy differentiation, then fit the same affine model and apply a unit conversion from deg/s to rad/s in the sensitivity term.

The UKF state is a unit quaternion orientation plus a 3D angular velocity, with uncertainty represented in a 6D tangent space. Sigma points are generated in this perturbation space, mapped to quaternions via axis--angle, and propagated using the measured time step with $$\mathbf{q}_{t+\Delta t} = \mathbf{q}_t \otimes \delta\mathbf{q}(\boldsymbol{\omega}\Delta t).$$ Angular velocity is updated additively.

Quaternion means are computed by iterative error averaging: relative rotations are mapped to axis--angle errors, averaged, and applied until the mean error is small. This produces a valid mean orientation and a covariance consistent with the manifold.

The measurement combines accelerometer and gyroscope readings. Accelerometer prediction uses gravity in the body frame, $$\hat{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{q}) \approx \mathbf{q}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{g} \otimes \mathbf{q},$$ while the gyroscope measurement is direct angular velocity. The UKF update uses the predicted measurement mean and covariance to compute the Kalman gain and applies a multiplicative correction to the quaternion.

The Kalman update is performed in the tangent space. I compute the innovation and measurement covariance, $$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y}_{\text{meas}} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \quad \mathbf{S} = \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{y}) + \mathbf{Q},$$ and the gain $$\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{P}_{xy}\mathbf{S}^{-1}.$$ The correction is $$\delta\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{r}, \quad \delta\mathbf{v} = [\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta\boldsymbol{\omega}],$$ applied by $$\mathbf{q} \leftarrow \delta\mathbf{q}(\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}) \otimes \mathbf{q}, \quad \boldsymbol{\omega} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\omega} + \delta\boldsymbol{\omega}.$$ The covariance update is $$\mathbf{P} \leftarrow \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{K}^\top.$$

I set the initial covariance and noise as diagonal matrices: $\Sigma$ uses ones on the diagonal for moderate initial uncertainty, $\mathbf{Q}$ uses 0.1s to represent process/model noise, and $\mathbf{R}$ uses 0.01s to represent measurement noise after calibration.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: Calibration yields consistent bias and sensitivity estimates across axes, and the resulting roll/pitch reconstructions track motion-capture angles closely in all three datasets.

With calibrated sensors, the UKF produces smooth angular-velocity estimates and quaternion trajectories that follow motion-capture ground truth. The roll, pitch, and yaw plots show tight alignment for roll/pitch, with yaw more sensitive to calibration and noise settings.

Figure I compares roll and pitch derived from calibrated acceleration to motion-capture ground truth across datasets. The alignment indicates the bias/scale fit is consistent and the axis conventions are correct.

Figure II shows calibrated gyroscope traces against ground-truth angular velocities for dataset 1. The overall amplitude and phase agreement confirm the scale and bias terms are reasonable across axes.
Figure III compares raw gyroscope readings to UKF angular-velocity estimates for dataset 2. The UKF output is smoother and less noisy while preserving the dominant motion trends.
Figure IV compares quaternion estimates to motion-capture quaternions on dataset 2. Agreement in the quaternion components indicates stable propagation and update behavior over time.
Figure V shows roll, pitch, and yaw against ground truth for dataset 2. Roll and pitch stay tightly aligned, while yaw shows the largest deviations consistent with gyro-driven drift.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Overall performance is strong in roll and pitch, which are tightly constrained by the gravity vector and respond well to calibration. Yaw remains the most sensitive axis and shows the largest deviations, consistent with reliance on gyroscope integration and its calibration quality.

The calibration stage is the dominant driver of filter accuracy. Small gyro scale or bias errors manifest quickly as yaw drift, while accelerometer biases shift static alignment. With the chosen noise settings, the filter balances smoothness and responsiveness, but yaw performance suggests further tuning of gyro sensitivity and noise could yield improvements.
